name: Amazon EC2
summary: AWS’s virtual machines: pick an instance type, boot an image, and you have a server in minutes.
intro: An EC2 instance is a virtual machine running on an AWS server. You choose an instance type, which fixes its vCPUs, memory, network bandwidth and sometimes a GPU or local SSD, and an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) to boot from. AWS offers more than 1,000 instance types across Intel, AMD and its own Arm-based Graviton chips. The instance’s disks are usually EBS volumes attached over the network, and it sits in a subnet of your VPC.

EC2 runs on the AWS Nitro System, which moves networking, storage and hypervisor work onto dedicated cards so nearly all of the host’s CPU goes to your instances. What sets EC2 apart is the purchasing model as much as the machine: On-Demand is billed per second (60-second minimum) on Linux and Windows, Savings Plans cut the price by up to 72% for a one- or three-year spend commitment, and Spot Instances sell spare capacity at up to 90% off, but AWS can take them back with a two-minute warning.
strengths: Full control: any OS, kernel settings, drivers or long-running daemon you like
Huge range of shapes, from burstable `t` instances to multi-GPU and terabyte-memory machines
Spot and Savings Plans make steady or interruptible work much cheaper than On-Demand list prices
The base layer most other AWS compute (ECS, EKS nodes, EMR) runs on
limits: You patch, secure and monitor the operating system yourself
Capacity is per instance, so you pay for idle CPU unless you add autoscaling
Booting a new instance takes tens of seconds to minutes, too slow for sudden spikes
Spot Instances can be reclaimed at any time, so the work on them must tolerate interruption

snippet.title: Launch a Graviton Spot instance with the AWS CLI

story: In 2003, Benjamin Black, a network engineering manager at Amazon, and his boss Chris Pinkham wrote a short paper describing infrastructure that was “completely standardized, completely automated, and relied extensively on web services”. Near the end they floated selling virtual servers as a service. In early 2004 Jeff Bezos asked for a detailed write-up of that idea, and the team turned it into a press release and FAQ for what became EC2.

Pinkham returned to South Africa, taking a lead developer with him, and built the EC2 team there. On August 25, 2006, Amazon opened a limited public beta. There was one kind of machine, later called the `m1.small`: the equivalent of a 1.7 GHz Xeon, 1.75 GB of RAM, 160 GB of local disk and 250 Mb/s of network, for 10 cents an hour, carved out of a physical server by the Xen hypervisor. EC2 dropped its beta label on October 23, 2008.

EC2 made a server something you rent by the hour from an API call rather than buy, rack and depreciate. Much of its later history is about wringing more out of the same hardware: auctioning spare capacity, replacing Xen with AWS’s own Nitro cards, and designing its own Arm chips.

choices.choice: Servers started and stopped by a web service call
choices.why: The original vision was infrastructure run entirely through automated web services. Exposing that to customers meant a machine could exist for an hour and be thrown away, billed only for the time it ran.

choices.choice: Local disks that disappear with the instance
choices.why: The first instances only had disk on the host itself, which is lost when the instance ends. Persistent storage was missing until EBS added network-attached volumes in 2008, which is why EBS is the default disk today.

choices.choice: Selling spare capacity at a discount
choices.why: A cloud has to keep idle machines ready for peaks. Spot Instances (2009) let customers bid on that unused capacity, on the understanding that AWS can take it back.

choices.choice: Moving the hypervisor’s work onto dedicated hardware
choices.why: Under Xen, emulating network and storage devices ate whole CPU cores, and the cost grew as networks and disks got faster. The Nitro System (2017) moved that work onto separate cards so customers get nearly all of the host’s CPU.
